tier_reason: Upgraded D to A: Eigen's official site now has a benchmark page (dated 2026-09-21) that compares Eigen with OpenBLAS 0.3.26, Intel oneMKL 2025.3 and BLIS 2.1. It states the CPU (Intel Xeon Gold 6444Y), the compiler and flags (GCC 13.3.0, -O3 -DNDEBUG -mavx512dq -mfma) and the method (Google Benchmark 1.8.3, 10 repetitions, median). The harness code is public in Eigen merge request !2903 under benchmarks/comparison/ (for example bench_gemm_compare.cpp and run.py).

corrections.workload: Single-threaded float and double BLAS operations (AXPY, DOT, GEMV, GEMM, TRSM, SYRK) and LAPACK operations (POTRF, GETRF, GEQRF, SYEV, GESDD, GEEV), measured over square and rectangular shapes. The Eigen arm uses no external BLAS. It is compared with OpenBLAS 0.3.26 (one thread, bundled LAPACK), Intel oneMKL 2025.3 (sequential) and BLIS 2.1 (BLAS only). Method: Google Benchmark 1.8.3, 10 repetitions of at least 0.2 s each, median GFLOP/s per cell, 874 operation-shape cells.
corrections.claimed_speedup: The page reports the geometric mean of Eigen/OpenBLAS rate ratios for square shapes in each size band (above 1 means Eigen is faster). Double-precision bands are n<=16 / 24-128 / 192-1024 / 1536-16384. Results: GEMM 1.11 / 0.85 / 1.07 / 0.94. GEMV 2.23 / 1.63 / 1.08 / 1.07. DOT 4.90 / 2.44 / 1.10 / 1.03. TRSM 1.48 / 3.60 / 2.19 / 1.23. POTRF 1.38 / 1.25 / 1.50 / 1.25. SYEV 1.36 / 1.77 / 2.33 / 1.79. Eigen is slower on GEEV (0.45 at 192-1024) and on GESDD (0.60 / 0.80 / 0.90 at 24-16384). Compared with oneMKL, Eigen wins mostly at small sizes. At large sizes it is often slower (double GEMM 0.93, SYEV 0.37, GEEV 0.41 at 192-1024). A companion Zen 5 page (WSL2) shows double GEMM against OpenBLAS at 1.28 / 0.95 / 1.30 / 1.21.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.3.0, -O3 -DNDEBUG -mavx512dq -mfma, C++17; Eigen upstream master ab4f7316d with no external BLAS and no OpenMP
corrections.hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6444Y, one socket, 16 cores / 32 threads, bare metal. Benchmark pinned to one logical CPU (single-threaded, AVX-512). Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS, Linux 6.17.0-35-generic. Performance governor; frequency not locked.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 1,190 GitLab stars (GitLab project created 2019-11-21); foundational dependency of ROS, TensorFlow, Ceres Solver, PCL, OpenCV, g2o, Blender, and many other numerical/robotics/vision projects
corrections.caveats: The Eigen team published this benchmark on its own site, and the harness is still in an open (unmerged) merge request, !2903. Results are mixed. Against OpenBLAS, Eigen is faster at small and medium sizes for level-1/2 BLAS and for several LAPACK operations (TRSM, POTRF, SYEV). For large GEMM and SYRK it is roughly at parity or slightly slower, and it is slower on GEEV and on mid-size GESDD. Against Intel oneMKL, Eigen is generally slower at large sizes. All measurements are single-threaded with frequency not locked. The older eigen.tuxfamily.org Benchmark page (BTL harness, March 2011) is now marked as a historical record.

notes: The published page loads at libeigen.gitlab.io. Its source is public at gitlab.com/libeigen/libeigen.gitlab.io under content/en/benchmarks/, with 5 September 2026 pages (Xeon, Zen 5, Apple M4). The metric field ('other') cannot be corrected here; the page measures throughput in GFLOP/s. The GitLab API confirmed license MPL-2.0, not archived, and a last commit on 2026-09-23 (PDT). The record's claim that Eigen 'moved off GitHub' is not supported, so I removed it.

tier_reason: These are first-party numbers from the author's blog, produced with the repo's own benchmarks/benchmarks.cpp. The CPU models are stated, but the optimization flags are not, and the g++ version is not stated for the AWS runs. This is C under the own-benchmark-with-partial-methodology rule, and the 226x figure is capped at C anyway because flags are unstated.

corrections.claimed_speedup: 8-core AWS c1.xlarge, balanced workload, 8 threads: moodycamel (with tokens) 795.01k ops/s vs boost::lockfree::queue 647.96k ops/s (~1.23x, derived from page data) vs tbb::concurrent_queue 692.97k ops/s (~1.15x, derived from page data). Only-enqueue (all producers), 8 threads: moodycamel with tokens (single-item enqueue, not bulk) 65.56M ops/s vs boost::lockfree 289.71k ops/s (~226x, derived from page data) vs tbb 936.20k ops/s (~70x, derived from page data). Overall weighted average ops/s/thread: moodycamel (including bulk) 19.04M vs boost::lockfree 4.07M (~4.7x, derived from page data) vs tbb 5.09M (~3.7x, derived from page data). The 32-core cc2.8xlarge run gives 18.50M vs 3.27M vs 4.21M. LockBasedQueue (a naive linked-list queue guarded by std::mutex) degrades in the balanced test from 2.6149us/op at 2 threads to 0.1120ms/op at 16 threads.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: g++ (version not stated for the AWS runs; 'g++ 4.81' stated for the Linode/Fedora 19 and MinGW-w64 netbook runs); optimization flags not stated on the blog page
corrections.hardware: AWS c1.xlarge: 8-core Intel Xeon E5506 @ 2.13GHz, Ubuntu. AWS cc2.8xlarge: 32-core Intel Xeon E5-2670 @ 2.60GHz, Ubuntu. Also a Linode VM, 8-core Intel Xeon E5-2650L @ 1.80GHz, Fedora 19. Also a dual-core AMD C-50 @ 1.0GHz netbook, Windows 7.
corrections.caveats: This is a first-party benchmark: the author's 2014 blog post plus the repo's own benchmarks/ directory. The blog compares against Boost 1.55 lockfree::queue and TBB 4.3 concurrent_queue, which are now old versions. Optimization flags are not stated. The 226x only-enqueue figure compares single-item enqueue with tokens against boost; it is not a bulk operation. However, it is an extreme-contention producer-only microbenchmark. The overall weighted averages include moodycamel's bulk operations, which boost and tbb do not support, so they are not like-for-like. LockBasedQueue is a hand-written linked list guarded by std::mutex, not std::queue.

notes: All claimed numbers are on the page and belong to the correct rows. The original record wrongly attributed 65.56M to bulk enqueue and did not mark its ratios as derived; both are fixed. GitHub reports license NOASSERTION. LICENSE.md confirms a dual license, Simplified BSD or Boost Software License 1.0. Other checks: 12,493 stars, not archived, not a fork, last commit 2026-07-11.

tier_reason: ScyllaDB, an independent third party, ran fio (a well-known benchmark tool) comparing io_uring with linux-aio, sync reads and posix-aio. The workload is described precisely, but the CPU model, kernel version, fio version and flags are not given, so the result falls short of A.

corrections.stars_or_usage: 3.8k stars; the standard userspace helper library for Linux io_uring, used by QEMU, RocksDB, ScyllaDB/Seastar, and many other async-I/O consumers
corrections.caveats: The page benchmarks the kernel io_uring interface, not liburing itself. fio's io_uring engine (engines/io_uring.c) issues raw io_uring_enter syscalls and does not link liburing. The win is therefore attributable to the interface that liburing wraps. The canonical evidence, Jens Axboe's 'Efficient IO with io_uring' paper at kernel.dk/io_uring.pdf, could not be opened because of a TLS certificate/hostname mismatch on kernel.dk. The CPU model, kernel version, fio version and compiler flags are not stated. Gains over linux-aio are modest (~7-12% direct I/O; ~22% buffered, where linux-aio degrades to synchronous behaviour). The larger win is over synchronous read/write and especially over thread-pool POSIX aio.

notes: All IOPS, MB/s and latency figures match Tables 1-2 and the Optane block on the ScyllaDB page, and the ratios are marked as derived. The license was corrected: all source files carry SPDX MIT, the README says 'dual licensed LGPL and MIT', and liburing.spec says 'LGPLv2+' (so not LGPL-2.1-only). I removed 'fio' from the list of users because fio does not use liburing.

tier_reason: The README table uses lzbench, a public, well-known third-party suite, and states GCC 8.2.0 and a Core i7-9700K. However, it does not state the compile flags or the lzbench version, and the rule says missing flags means not A. This is B because the win comes from a well-known independent benchmark suite.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC v8.2.0 (lzbench build; lzbench version and optimization flags not stated in README)
corrections.caveats: The license is split by directory: lib/ (the codec) is BSD-2-Clause, and the CLI, tests and examples are GPL-2.0-or-later. Both are OSI-approved, so the library is copyable. The numbers are reported first-party in the README from an lzbench run of LZ4 v1.9.0 against zlib 1.2.11. The compiler, CPU and OS are stated, but the compile flags and the lzbench version are not, so the evidence is not tier A. LZ4 wins on speed at a lower compression ratio than zlib -1 (2.101 vs 2.730). Independent corroboration: the lzbench README (lzbench 2.0.1, gcc 14.2.0, AMD EPYC 9554) lists lz4 1.10.0 at 577/3716 MB/s against zlib 1.3.1 -1 at 93.0/323 MB/s. License: the library (lib/) is BSD-2-Clause; the command-line programs (programs/) are GPL-2.0-or-later.

notes: All numbers match the README Benchmarks table, and the ratios are correctly marked as derived. Usability changed from 'mixed' to 'copyable' because every file is under an OSI license (BSD-2-Clause or GPL-2.0-or-later) and none is unlicensed. last_commit is taken from the default branch 'dev' (2026-06-01); the 2026-07-01 value was the repo pushed_at date.
